chapter_title: Concerning the worn and torn apart Garments, or the tattered Clothes, or the Elements, the Cross, and the rest too
chapter_note: A remarkably clean teaching chapter. The substrate dominates: a systematic terminological exposition mapping seven names for the devoured light to their cosmic referents. No editorial bridge material, no exhortation, no institutional content. The editorial layer is confined entirely to the dialogue frame (¶1, 4, 5, 6) and minor framing phrases in ¶2, 3, 7. The teaching structure is: (1) enumerate terms as questions, (2) define each term by mapping name→cosmic entity/condition, (3) conclude with restoration theology. Every mapping stays within the cosmic system. The 'we have proclaimed/termed/called' self-referential phrases in ¶8-12 are part of the systematic definitional voice, not editorial insertions.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Pure formulaic opening: 'Once more the apostle is sitting in the congregation of his disciples.' Standard Kephalaia session marker with no cosmological content.

paragraphs.core_text: what then are these 'great garments'? Or again, this you sometimes call the 'rags', what are those 'rags'? Or the 'worn and torn apart'? Or what are the 'images and the tattered clothes'? Or what is this name: 'light element'? Or conversely, what is the 'Cross of Light'? Or why named otherwise: the 'counsel of life'? Or what is the 'soul that is slain'; being killed, oppressed, and murdered in the enemy? What are all these names?
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed 'What is this lesson that is written in the scriptures? It proclaims the name the "great garments", but' — scripture reference framing that wraps the substantive cosmological question. The reference to 'scriptures' anchors to the Manichaean textual canon, not the cosmic system.
paragraphs.temporal_note: The enumeration of seven cosmological terms as questions defines the entire teaching structure of this chapter. These are substantive cosmological questions in the Persian pedagogical tradition. The 'written in the scriptures' framing is editorial but the term-list itself is substrate — each term answered systematically in ¶7-14.

paragraphs.core_text: how have they changed with all these names and become set in altered forms
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed 'Look, they are written and sealed, according to memory, by a multitude of scriptures.' (scripture reference framing), 'Now then I ask you, so that you may tell me: What are they? Or' (dialogue frame), and trailing 'namely all these?' (redundant frame). Kept the substantive cosmological question about transformation.
paragraphs.temporal_note: This question asks HOW the light came to have different names and forms — a different question from ¶2's WHAT. It is answered in the concluding ¶15. The 'written and sealed... by a multitude of scriptures' is clearly editorial reference to Manichaean canon.
Pure dialogue transition formula: 'His disciples say to him:'

Purely honorific disciple response with no cosmological content. 'Source of all wisdoms,' 'fount of all wisdoms' — hagiographic address. The disciples' deflection back to the teacher is a standard dialogue convention.
Pure formula: 'Then speaks the apostle to them:' with manuscript page marker ⟨p.177⟩.

paragraphs.core_text: The garments that are named 'great garment' are the five intellectuals that make perfect the body of the Pillar of Glory, the Perfect Man. They were purified by the coming of the Ambassador.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed 'It is proper for you to understand this.' — pedagogical address formula directed at the audience, not part of the cosmological definition.
paragraphs.temporal_note: First definition in the series: 'great garment' = five intellectuals of the Pillar of Glory / Perfect Man. Both sides of the mapping are cosmic entities. The five intellectuals, the Pillar of Glory, the Perfect Man, and the Ambassador are all cosmic-system beings. This is the purest substrate form: name→cosmic referent.

paragraphs.core_text: In contrast, the ones named 'rag': the rags are the devoured enlightening power. It is compounded and entangled in the body of the universe in the rulers who are above, who exist in all the firmaments. Also, its shine is that which lights up and is displayed in the stars of the chain and the powers of the course. And likewise, these rags that are entangled in these three earths below, above the head of the Porter [...] on the earth that is under the Porter. These are named the 'rags', because [...] set [...]
paragraphs.temporal_note: Second definition: 'rags' = devoured enlightening power distributed throughout the cosmic structure. Maps into firmaments, stars of the chain, powers of the course, three earths, the Porter — all cosmic geography. Lacunae at end indicate manuscript damage. The 'stars of the chain' and 'powers of the course' are technical cosmological terms for astral bodies in the cosmic mechanism.

paragraphs.core_text: However, the 'great worn and torn apart garments', which we have proclaimed, is this entangled living power. It is reaped, cut, and devoured. It is overpowered by the five worlds of the flesh, which creep as they move from place to place.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Third definition: 'worn and torn apart' = entangled living power consumed by the five worlds of flesh. The 'five worlds of the flesh' are the five archontic species — a core cosmological category. 'which we have proclaimed' is the systematic teaching voice referring back to the enumeration, not editorial insertion.

paragraphs.core_text: On the other hand, [these] we have termed the 'images and the great tattered clothes' [...] are the three great garments of the wind, the fire, and the water. These the Living Spirit cloaked upon his body. With them he set in order things in the universe. With them also he emptied the vessels. He swept them out and laid them bare in front of the Porter at the foundation of all things.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Fourth definition: 'images and tattered clothes' = the three elemental garments (wind, fire, water) that the Living Spirit used to structure the cosmos. Maps name→cosmic elements→cosmic agent's action. All within the cosmic system: Living Spirit, vessels, Porter, foundation — all cosmic architecture.

paragraphs.core_text: Conversely, '[the ele]ments', we have called them this name, are this power that remains in all things below. It rises up in the wombs of all the earths, gathering together, and pouring forth upon all things.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Fifth definition: 'elements' = the power remaining in things below, rising through the earths. Describes a cosmic process — the light ascending through the cosmic structure. 'wombs of all the earths' is correspondential language mapping reproductive processes onto cosmic geography.

paragraphs.core_text: And then, the '[Light] Cross' [we have termed] this bound 'light power'. It [...] all [...] upon the earth, in the dry and the moist.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Sixth definition: 'Light Cross' = bound light power in earth, dry and moist. Despite lacunae, the structure is clear: name→cosmic condition. The 'dry and moist' are elemental qualities within the cosmic system, not contemporary references.

paragraphs.core_text: Also, the one named the 'counsel of life' is the summons and the obedience. It moves in all these powers that we have named. It awakens them, gives them ease, and drives them to their movement.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Seventh definition: 'counsel of life' = the summons and the obedience. These are cosmic entities (the Call and the Answer) that animate the other light-forms. This maps name→cosmic agent→cosmic function. The summons/obedience pair is a fundamental correspondential structure — the call from above and the response from below.

paragraphs.core_text: The one named 'the soul that is slain', which is killed, oppressed and murdered; it is this power of fruit, vegetables and seeds. They shall be threshed, plucked and cut down; and they give nourishment to the worlds of the flesh. Further: the wood should it be dry, and the garment should it become ragged, will perish. Again, it is [a pa]rt of this entire soul that is slain and killed; since also even this whole part of it they kill [...]
paragraphs.temporal_note: Eighth definition: 'soul that is slain' = power in vegetation (fruit, vegetables, seeds). The description of threshing, plucking, cutting describes cosmic processes — how the light trapped in vegetation is consumed by the worlds of flesh. The wood/garment analogy extends the teaching within the natural-correspondential register. Both sides remain within the cosmic system.

paragraphs.core_text: For all these names [...] are a single [...] since the beginning, it [...] as it enlightens; but they separated into all these parts in this first contest. They became set in all these altered forms, and these many names. Of course, if now all these varieties are laid bare, and stripped of all these appearances, and parted from all these names; they will gather together and make a single form, and a single name, unaltered and unchangeable for ever in the land of their first essence, from which they were sent forth against the enemy.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Cosmological conclusion answering ¶3's question (how did they change?): all names are one light, separated in the first cosmic contest, to be restored to unity in the land of first essence. 'The first contest,' 'the land of their first essence,' 'sent forth against the enemy' — entirely cosmic-historical. This is the teaching's resolution: multiplicity of names reflects the differentiation of light in mixture; restoration returns to unity. No editorial extension, no exhortation — the chapter ends on the teaching itself.
